subject: old laboratory notebook
title: Marie Curie's Notebooks Are Too Radioactive to Touch, 90 Years Later

scenes.text: Marie Curie's notebooks are still too radioactive to touch.
They sit in lead-lined boxes at France's national library. To read one, you sign a liability waiver and put on protective clothing.
Curie carried tubes of radium in her coat pocket and kept bottles of it in her desk drawer, fascinated by the glow.
Her papers, her furniture, even her cookbooks are contaminated. Radium-226 has a half-life of about 1,600 years.
She died in 1934, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia, blamed on decades of handling radiation.
Her notes will stay dangerous for another 1,500 years. Roughly 50 more generations before anyone reads them bare-handed.

description:
Marie Curie's laboratory notebooks are still radioactive, and will be for about another 1,500 years.
They are stored in lead-lined boxes at the Bibliothèque nationale de France; anyone who wants to consult them signs a liability waiver and wears protective clothing. Curie carried test tubes of radium in her coat pocket and kept samples in her desk drawer, and her papers, furniture and even her cookbooks remain contaminated: radium-226 has a half-life of about 1,601 years. She died in 1934, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia attributed to her research.
Would you sign the waiver to read them?
first_comment: Lead boxes, a waiver and a hazmat suit, just to read a notebook. Which historical object would you most want to hold?
